# Task 3

## Part A

Universal Pictures was selected as the external benchmark for Meridian Pictures because its historical production budgets provide a reference point for understanding competitor spending. After filtering the dataset to Universal Pictures films and excluding records with missing, non-finite or non-positive budgets, 260 films were retained for the descriptive analysis.

The summary statistics show a mean production budget of approximately \$41.57 million, a median of \$30.50 million, and a standard deviation of approximately \$37.89 million. The mean is higher than the median, suggesting that a relatively small number of high-budget films raise the average. The substantial standard deviation also indicates considerable variation in production spending across films.

These results suggest that a single average budget may not adequately represent the range of production costs. A probability distribution is therefore useful for modelling the variation in budgets and estimating the likelihood of different spending levels.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: true
#| include: false

# Fitting in the data with normal distribution

Universal_budget <- assignment_data |>
  dplyr::filter(primary_company == "Universal Pictures") |>
  dplyr::select(title, id, status, primary_genre, budget) |>
  dplyr::mutate(budget = as.double(budget))

#checking for any negative, zero or other anomaly in budget

Universal_budget |>
  summarise(
    total_films = n(),
    missing_budgets = sum(is.na(budget)),
    zero_budgets = sum(budget == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    negative_budgets = sum(budget < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    positive_budgets = sum(budget > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )


#Summary statistics

budget_summary <- Universal_budget |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_budget = mean(budget, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_budget = median(budget, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_budget = sd(budget, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

#creating the table out of the summary statistics

budget_summary |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Universal Pictures Production Budget Summary",
    subtitle = "Descriptive statistics of historical film budgets"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    n = "Number of Films",
    mean_budget = "Mean Budget (USD)",
    median_budget = "Median Budget (USD)",
    sd_budget = "Standard Deviation (USD)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(mean_budget, median_budget, sd_budget),
    decimals = 2,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = n,
    decimals = 0,
    use_seps = TRUE
  ) |>
  opt_row_striping() |>
  opt_table_outline() |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Source: Historical Universal Pictures film budget data."
)

```

## Assessment of the Normal Distribution

The histogram of Universal Pictures' production budgets shows a positively skewed distribution. Most films have budgets concentrated at the lower end, while a smaller number of productions have substantially higher budgets, creating a long right tail.

The fitted normal curve does not adequately represent this pattern. A normal distribution is symmetric around its mean, whereas the observed budgets are strongly right-skewed. The dashed vertical line marks the mean budget of approximately \$41.57 million, which lies to the right of the main concentration of observations.

This mismatch suggests that the normal distribution may be an unrealistic model for Universal Pictures' production budgets. In particular, it may misrepresent the probabilities of lower and exceptionally high budgets. Alternative distributions designed to accommodate positive, right-skewed data should therefore be considered.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: true
#plotting the graph 

ggplot(Universal_budget, aes(x = budget)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 30,
    fill = "skyblue",
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(
      mean = mean(Universal_budget$budget, na.rm= TRUE),
      sd= sd(Universal_budget$budget, na.rm= TRUE)
      
    ),
    colour = "brown",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean(Universal_budget$budget, na.rm = TRUE),
    colour = "darkblue",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Universal Pictures Production Budgets",
    subtitle = "Histogram with fitted normal distribution",
    x = "Production Budget (USD)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

## Choice of the alternative distribution and modelling

To identify a realistic probability model, normal, log-normal, Gamma, Exponential and Weibull distributions were considered. Their fitted curves and Q-Q plots were used to assess how closely the theoretical distributions represented the observed budgets, while AIC was used to compare their relative fit. The final model will be selected based on the AIC results and supporting diagnostic plots.

**Note :Budgets were then divided by 10,000,000 to improve numerical convenience during model estimation while preserving their relative distribution.**

```{r}
Universal_budget_clean <- Universal_budget |>
  filter(
    !is.na(budget),
    is.finite(budget),
    budget > 0
  ) |>
  mutate(budget_millions = budget / 10000000)

budget_values <- Universal_budget_clean$budget_millions


gamma_fit <- fitdistr(
  budget_values,
  "gamma"
)

weibull_fit <- fitdistr(
  budget_values,
  "weibull"
)

exponential_fit <- fitdistr(
  budget_values,
  "exponential"
)

```

## Graphical Representation of Model Choice

@fig-budget-distributions compares the Gamma, Exponential and Weibull distributions fitted to Universal Pictures' production budgets. The observed budgets are positively skewed, with most films concentrated at lower budget levels and a smaller number of films having substantially higher budgets.

The Gamma and Weibull distributions appear to capture the overall shape of the histogram reasonably well, including its peak and long right tail. The Exponential distribution declines more sharply from the lower end and appears to represent the concentration of budgets around the peak less accurately.

```{r}
#| label: fig-budget-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of fitted Gamma, Exponential and Weibull distributions for Universal Pictures' production budgets."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| output: true
#plotting the three fits in histogram

make_plot <- function(curve, distribution_name, curve_colour) {

  ggplot(
    data.frame(budget_values = budget_values),
    aes(x = budget_values)
  ) +

    geom_histogram(
      aes(y = after_stat(density)),
      bins = 30,
      fill = "skyblue",
      colour = "black"
    ) +

    stat_function(
      fun = curve,
      colour = curve_colour,
      linewidth = 1.2,
      args = switch(
        distribution_name,

        "Gamma" = list(
          shape = gamma_fit$estimate["shape"],
          rate = gamma_fit$estimate["rate"]
        ),

        "Exponential" = list(
          rate = exponential_fit$estimate["rate"]
        ),

        "Weibull" = list(
          shape = weibull_fit$estimate["shape"],
          scale = weibull_fit$estimate["scale"]
        )
      )
    ) +

    labs(
      title = distribution_name,
      x = NULL,
      y = "Density"
    ) +

    theme_minimal() +

    theme(
      axis.title.x = element_blank()
    )
}


# Create the three plots
p_gamma <- make_plot(
  dgamma, "Gamma", "red"
)

p_exponential <- make_plot(
  dexp, "Exponential", "blue"
)

p_weibull <- make_plot(
  dweibull, "Weibull", "darkgreen"
)

combined_plot <- (
  p_gamma | p_exponential | p_weibull
) +

  plot_annotation(
    title = "Universal Pictures Production Budgets",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Comparison of fitted Gamma, Exponential",
      "and Weibull distributions"
    ),
    caption = "Budget (Units of USD 10 Million)"
  ) &

  theme(
    plot.caption = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,
      size = 11,
      colour = "black"
    )
  )


# Display the final figure
combined_plot

```

The @fig-budget-qq compare the observed production budgets of Universal Pictures with the fitted Gamma, Exponential and Weibull distributions. The Gamma and Weibull distributions align more closely with the reference line across most of the budget range, although both deviate for higher-budget films. The Exponential distribution shows greater deviation, suggesting a weaker fit. Overall, the plots indicate that Gamma and Weibull are more suitable for modelling production budgets, with Gamma appearing to provide a slightly better fit.

```{r}
#| label: fig-budget-qq
#| fig-cap: "Q-Q plots comparing Gamma, Exponential and Weibull distributions fitted to Universal Pictures' production budgets."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| output: true


n <- length(budget_values)
p <- ppoints(n)
observed <- sort(budget_values)

# Gamma Q-Q plot data
gamma_qq <- data.frame(
  theoretical = qgamma(
    p,
    shape = gamma_fit$estimate["shape"],
    rate = gamma_fit$estimate["rate"]
  ),
  observed = observed
)

# Exponential Q-Q plot data
exponential_qq <- data.frame(
  theoretical = qexp(
    p,
    rate = exponential_fit$estimate["rate"]
  ),
  observed = observed
)

# Weibull Q-Q plot data
weibull_qq <- data.frame(
  theoretical = qweibull(
    p,
    shape = weibull_fit$estimate["shape"],
    scale = weibull_fit$estimate["scale"]
  ),
  observed = observed
)


# Function to create each Q-Q plot
make_qq_plot <- function(qq_data, distribution_name) {

  ggplot(
    qq_data,
    aes(x = theoretical, y = observed)
  ) +
    geom_point(size = 1.5) +
    geom_abline(
      intercept = 0,
      slope = 1,
      colour = "red",
      linewidth = 0.7
    ) +
    labs(
      title = distribution_name,
      x = NULL,
      y = "Observed Quantiles"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.title.x = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(
        face = "bold",
        hjust = 0.5
      )
    )
}


# Create individual plots
qq_gamma <- make_qq_plot(
  gamma_qq, "Gamma"
)

qq_exponential <- make_qq_plot(
  exponential_qq, "Exponential"
)

qq_weibull <- make_qq_plot(
  weibull_qq, "Weibull"
)


# Combine all three Q-Q plots
combined_qq <- (
  qq_gamma | qq_exponential | qq_weibull
) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Q-Q Plot Comparison of Production Budget Distributions",
    subtitle = "Universal Pictures | Budgets in units of USD 10 million",
    caption = "The red line represents theoretical agreement."
  ) &
  theme(
    plot.caption = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,
      size = 10
    )
  )

# Display the combined figure
combined_qq
```

## Comparing the AIC for Decision making

The AIC results indicate that the Gamma distribution provides the best relative fit for Universal Pictures’ production budgets, with a score of 1201.090. The Weibull distribution performs almost equally well (1201.542), while the Exponential distribution has a higher AIC (1213.346), indicating a weaker fit. For Meridian Pictures, Gamma is therefore the preferred model for estimating historical budget patterns, although Weibull remains a reasonable alternative.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: true

aic_table <- data.frame(
  Distribution = c(
    "Gamma",
    "Exponential",
    "Weibull"
  ),
  AIC = c(
    AIC(gamma_fit),
    AIC(exponential_fit),
    AIC(weibull_fit)
  )
)

#creating the table to see clearly

aic_table |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparison of Fitted Distributions",
    subtitle = "Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Distribution = "Distribution",
    AIC = "AIC Value"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = AIC,
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = AIC,
      rows = AIC == min(AIC)
    )
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Lower AIC values indicate a better relative model fit."
  )



```

## Part B

Action films from all studios were selected to assess the downside risk of the Action genre. The data was checked for missing, zero, negative and infinite values across numeric variables.

Films with zero budgets were identified because ROI cannot be reliably calculated when the budget is zero. Missing and infinite ROI values were excluded from the analysis, while valid zero and negative ROI values were retained because they may represent genuine financial outcomes.

```{r data cleaning for action}

glimpse(assignment_data)


#filtering data
action_data <- assignment_data |>
  filter(
    primary_genre == "Action"
  )

#checking for negative, zero and NA in the filtered data

action_data|>
  summarise(
    across(
      where(is.numeric),
      list(
        NA_count = ~sum(is.na(.x)),
        zero_count = ~sum(.x == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
        negative_count = ~sum(.x < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
      )
    )
  )
#looking for negatives, 0 and infinte values in ROI variable

action_data |>
  summarise(
    total_films = n(),
    missing_ROI = sum(is.na(roi)),
    zero_ROI = sum(roi == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    infinite_ROI = sum(!is.finite(roi), na.rm = TRUE)
  )

#cleaning the action filtered data

infinite_row <- action_data |> 
  filter(budget == 0 & revenue > 0)

action_data_clean<- action_data |> mutate(
    revenue = ifelse(budget == 0, NA, revenue),
    budget = ifelse(budget==0, NA, budget),
    profit  = ifelse(budget == 0, NA, profit)
  )

```

The 25th percentile of ROI was estimated using non-parametric bootstrapping with 15,000 resamples. This method repeatedly resamples the observed ROI values with replacement, without assuming a specific probability distribution.

The estimated 25th percentile was 0.5764, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.4963 to 0.6596. This suggests that the lower-performing quarter of Action films has an ROI threshold of approximately 0.5764, with uncertainty reflected in the confidence interval.

```{r non parametric}
roi_values <- action_data_clean$roi

# Remove missing and infinite values
roi_values <- roi_values[
  !is.na(roi_values) & is.finite(roi_values)
]

# Estimating 25th percentile
q25 <- quantile(roi_values, probs = 0.25)

# Non-parametric bootstrap
set.seed(100)

B <- 15000
n <- length(roi_values)

bootstrap_q25 <- replicate(
  B,
  quantile(
    sample(roi_values, size = n, replace = TRUE),
    probs = 0.25,
    names = FALSE
  )
)

# Calculate the 95% confidence interval
bootstrap_CI <- quantile(
  bootstrap_q25,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.975)
)

# Display results
q25
bootstrap_CI
```

```{r parametric}

# Prepare ROI values
roi_values <- action_data_clean$roi

roi_values <- roi_values[
  !is.na(roi_values) & is.finite(roi_values)
]

# Fit a normal distribution
normal_fit <- fitdistr(roi_values, "normal")

mu <- normal_fit$estimate["mean"]
sigma <- normal_fit$estimate["sd"]

# Estimate the 25th percentile
q25_normal <- qnorm(
  0.25,
  mean = mu,
  sd = sigma
)

# Parametric bootstrap
set.seed(100)

B <- 15000
n <- length(roi_values)

parametric_q25 <- replicate(
  B,
  quantile(
    rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma),
    probs = 0.25,
    names = FALSE
  )
)

# Calculate the 95% confidence interval
parametric_CI <- quantile(
  parametric_q25,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.975)
)

# Display results
q25_normal
parametric_CI

```

# Part C

A normal parametric bootstrap was initially used to compare the results with the non-parametric method. The normal distribution accommodates both positive and negative ROI values, unlike the standard Gamma and Weibull distributions, which require strictly positive values. However, @fig-roi-normal shows substantial right-skewness, suggesting that the normality assumption may not be appropriate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-roi-normal
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of Action Film ROI compared with a fitted normal curve"
#| echo: false
#| output: true

roi_values <- action_data_clean$roi
roi_values <- roi_values[
  !is.na(roi_values) & is.finite(roi_values)
]

roi_data <- data.frame(roi = roi_values)

ggplot(roi_data, aes(x = roi)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 30,
    fill = "skyblue",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    args = list(
      mean = mean(roi_values),
      sd = sd(roi_values)
    ),
    colour = "red",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Action Film ROI",
    subtitle = "Histogram compared with a fitted normal curve",
    x = "ROI",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

As shown in @tbl-roi-comparison, the non-parametric bootstrap estimates the 25th percentile at 0.5764, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.4963–0.6596, while the normal parametric bootstrap estimates it at −0.8080.

The **non-parametric bootstrap** is preferred because it preserves the observed distribution without assuming normality. For Meridian Pictures, this provides a more defensible estimate of lower-end ROI, supporting investment decisions that account for the actual variation in Action-film returns.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-roi-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of 25th Percentile ROI Estimates and 95% Confidence Intervals"
#| echo: false
#| output: true

comparison_table <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Non-parametric bootstrap",
    "Normal parametric bootstrap"
  ),
  `25th Percentile` = c(
    as.numeric(q25),
    as.numeric(q25_normal)
  ),
  `Lower 95% CI` = c(
    as.numeric(bootstrap_CI[1]),
    as.numeric(parametric_CI[1])
  ),
  `Upper 95% CI` = c(
    as.numeric(bootstrap_CI[2]),
    as.numeric(parametric_CI[2])
  ),
  Suitability = c(
    "Preferred: preserves the observed ROI distribution",
    "Less suitable: assumes normally distributed ROI"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

comparison_table |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Comparison of Action Film ROI Estimates",
    subtitle = "25th Percentile and 95% Confidence Intervals"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      `25th Percentile`,
      `Lower 95% CI`,
      `Upper 95% CI`
    ),
    decimals = 4
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Method = "Estimation Method",
    `25th Percentile` = "Estimated Q25",
    `Lower 95% CI` = "Lower Limit",
    `Upper 95% CI` = "Upper Limit",
    Suitability = "Assessment"
  ) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = Method,
      rows = Method == "Non-parametric bootstrap"
    )
  )
```

## Part D

The method choices allow Meridian Pictures to use historical data to support financial planning. Universal Pictures' budgets are right-skewed, so a normal distribution may not represent them well. The Gamma distribution provides a suitable model for simulating Universal Pictures' right-skewed production budgets.

The non-parametric bootstrap estimates the lower-quarter revenue-to-budget ratio for Action films without assuming a normal distribution. The resulting estimate of 0.5764, with a confidence interval of approximately 0.467–0.676, gives the finance team a downside-risk benchmark and communicates its uncertainty. The ROI represented by the data is revenue divided by production budget, a ratio of 0.5764 means approximately 58 cents in revenue per \$1 of production budget. It does not mean a 58% profit or return.

It gives the finance team a benchmark for the downside risk associated with Action films. The confidence interval also shows the uncertainty around that estimate, rather than presenting it as an exact value.

Together, these results support more realistic budget simulations and more cautious assessment of potential Action film outcomes.
